how-much-to-charge-for-pool-service.html.text:
← Pool route pricing

How much to charge for monthly pool service

Pool service is priced per pool and costed per hour, and that mismatch is why a full route can stay busy without making money. The monthly rate a customer sees covers a visit; what the business actually spends is labour on the route — including every minute spent driving between stops, which no customer is billed for directly and most pricing leaves out entirely.

Open the free pool route pricing calculator

Price the route, then divide

  1. Route hours: accounts × visits per month × (service minutes + drive minutes) ÷ 60.
  2. Labour: route hours at your loaded hourly rate — the rate that includes payroll burden, not the wage.
  3. Chemicals per visit and overhead per account, added on top.
  4. Divide the route's total cost by accounts for cost per account, then by (1 − target margin) for the monthly price it has to carry.

Worked example

Forty accounts, four visits a month, 35 minutes of service and 12 minutes of driving per visit is 125.33 route hours a month. At $28 an hour that is $3,509.33 of labour; $18 of chemicals per visit adds $2,880.00 and $12 of overhead per account adds $480.00, for a route cost of $6,869.33 — about $171.73 per account. At a 35% target margin the route needs $10,568.21 a month, or $264.21 per account. Two figures are worth sitting with: the drive alone is 32 of those 125 hours, and marking the same cost up by 35% instead would have priced each account at $231.84 and quietly delivered 26% margin.

Common questions

How much should I charge per month for pool service?

Work out the route's monthly cost first, then divide. Add up service minutes and drive minutes per visit across every account and every visit in the month to get route hours, cost those hours at your loaded labour rate, add chemicals per visit and overhead per account, and that is what the route costs to run. Divide by your accounts for cost per account, then divide by one minus your target margin to get the monthly price each account has to carry. Pricing per pool without costing the drive is what makes a full route unprofitable.

Should drive time be included in pool route pricing?

Yes — it is paid time on the clock and often a third of the route. At 35 minutes of service and 12 minutes of driving per stop, roughly a quarter of every visit is spent getting there, so a price built only from service time under-recovers labour by that much on every account, every visit, all year. Drive time is also the figure that improves when a route tightens geographically, which is why it belongs in the model as its own input rather than buried in an hourly rate.

Why is my pool route busy but not profitable?

Usually because the price was set per pool against what competitors charge, while the cost is incurred per hour on the route. Adding an account that is fifteen minutes off the line adds far more cost than one on it, but both get quoted the same monthly rate, so a route can grow, fill the week, and earn less per hour than it did when it was smaller. Costing the whole route and dividing back out shows which accounts are carrying their drive and which are not.

How do I set a target margin on a service route?

Treat margin as a share of price, not a markup on cost: divide the cost per account by one minus the margin. At 35 percent, a cost of $171.73 needs a price of $264.21, not $231.84 — marking cost up by 35 percent yields about 26 percent margin, which is the most common arithmetic error in route pricing. Set the margin to cover what the cost lines do not: equipment replacement, callbacks, unpaid admin time, and the accounts that cancel.

Common questions

Does drive time between stops belong in the price?

Yes — drive minutes per visit is a required input, not an optional extra, because windshield time is paid time on a route even though no pool gets serviced during it. Skipping it or entering zero understates true monthly labor hours and produces a price that only covers time at the pool, not the route.

Why is the result called a “minimum” price instead of a recommended price?

The number is the floor at which your entered labor, drive time, chemicals, and overhead hit your target margin — it is not what the market will bear or what competitors charge. It also does not add taxes, equipment replacement, bad debt, or seasonal work (algae season, filter cleans, closings/openings) unless you fold those into your overhead or chemical inputs yourself.

What if visits per month vary by account (some weekly, some biweekly)?

Run the calculator per account group with different visit counts, or use a blended average across your route and treat the result as a route-wide floor rather than an exact account-by-account price. The tool prices one uniform account profile at a time; it does not segment a mixed route automatically.

Does anything about my accounts or pricing get uploaded?

No. Every number stays in this browser's local storage as a private draft, and a shareable link encodes the same inputs directly in the URL hash rather than on a server. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events like estimate, share-link, and current-price-checked, and you can turn it off with the button above.

vs-a-flat-per-pool-monthly-rate.html.text:
← Pool route pricing calculator

This calculator vs. a flat per-pool monthly rate

“$X a month per pool, every account” is not a price for a route — it is a price for one route's drive time and density, quietly applied to the next route regardless of how spread out it is.

What a flat per-pool rate is

A flat monthly rate per pool is the fastest way to quote: pick a round, competitive-sounding number and charge it on every account. It is easy to advertise, and it is the figure a homeowner holding a competitor's flyer will ask you to match.

The number behind it was usually set once, off one route — a particular mix of service minutes and drive time between stops — and then reused for every account after that, whether the next route runs tight streets a few minutes apart or spans a wider territory with more windshield time between pools.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter your accounts, visits per account per month, service minutes and drive minutes per visit, loaded labor rate, chemical cost, overhead per account, and target margin. It prices the route's true labor — service time and drive time together — plus chemicals and overhead, and returns a minimum monthly price per account for this route, not a flat number carried over from a different one.

What a flat per-pool rate doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same figure whether the route runs 12 minutes of drive between stops or 25, as long as the word "pool" applies. Prices route hours from your own service minutes plus drive minutes per visit, so a more spread-out route needs a higher price than a tight one.
Has no line for chemicals or overhead that vary by account — every pool is assumed to cost the plan's original account the same to service. Adds chemicals per visit and overhead per account as their own lines, so a heavier-demand pool or a higher-overhead account shows up in the price.
Gives the operator a number to quote, not a number to check an existing route against once it grows or its territory shifts. Accepts your current price and reports the actual margin and route profit it produces, so a route can be re-checked as it changes rather than trusted forever.
Treats margin as a markup on a remembered cost figure, which is a different and usually smaller number than margin as a share of price. Divides route cost by one minus the target margin, so the price actually clears the margin you set instead of falling short of it by a common arithmetic mistake.
Cannot say how much a shortfall is worth in dollars across the whole route. Multiplies the per-account gap by your account count, so a rate that is quietly short shows up as a monthly and annual number, not just a feeling.

Two routes, one flat rate

Using this calculator's own defaults for a 40-account route on 4 visits a month with 35 minutes of service per visit:

A tight route at 12 minutes of drive per visit runs 125.3 route hours a month, costs $6,869.33 to service, and this calculator prices it at $264.21 per account at a 35% target margin. Widen the same 40 accounts to a spread-out route at 25 minutes of drive per visit — nothing else changed — and route hours rise to 160.0, cost rises to $7,840.00, and the price needed to hit the same 35% target margin is $301.54 per account.

Quote the spread-out route the tight route's flat $264.21 instead and it clears only 25.8% margin, not 35% — short $37.33 per account per month, or $1,493.33 a month and $17,920.00 a year across the 40 accounts. The route is still above break-even, which is what makes the shortfall easy to miss: nothing about it looks like a losing route, it is simply a route earning ten points less margin than the operator believes it is.

Common questions

Why does a flat per-pool rate get route pricing wrong?

Because the cost driver is drive time between stops, not "has a pool." A tight 40-account route at 12 minutes of drive per visit costs $6,869.33 a month to run and needs $264.21 per account at a 35% target margin. The same 40 accounts spread across a wider territory at 25 minutes of drive per visit costs $7,840.00 a month and needs $301.54 per account. A flat rate set on the tight route and quoted to both charges the spread-out one $37.33 a month short on every account -- the same rate, two different routes.

What does a flat per-pool rate usually leave out entirely?

Drive time between stops, which is paid labor even though no pool is serviced during it. A rate quoted per pool, off a memorized going rate or a competitor's flyer, has no line that moves when the next route is more spread out, when chemicals run higher on a problem pool, or when overhead per account changes. It was set once, on one route's density, and reused regardless of the next one's.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

Using this calculator's own defaults for a 40-account route at 4 visits a month, 35 minutes of service and 12 minutes of drive per visit: the route costs $6,869.33 a month and needs $264.21 per account to hit a 35% target margin. Widen the same 40-account route to 25 minutes of drive per visit -- a more spread-out territory, nothing else changed -- and the route costs $7,840.00 a month and needs $301.54 per account. Quote the second route the first route's $264.21 flat rate and it clears only 25.8% margin instead of 35%, short $37.33 per account per month, or $1,493.33 a month and $17,920.00 a year across the 40 accounts -- and it is still above break-even, so nothing about the shortfall shows up as an obviously losing route.

Is a flat per-pool rate ever the right way to price a route?

For a narrow band of routes with genuinely similar density -- same visit frequency, similar drive time between stops, similar chemical demand -- a flat rate can land close. The risk is quoting it to the next route without checking whether that route is actually in the same band, because the flat number does not know the difference and neither does the operator until the drive time is added up.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates or what competing pool services charge. It takes your accounts, visits, service minutes, drive minutes, labor rate, chemical cost, overhead, and target margin, and turns them into a minimum monthly price for this route -- the arithmetic a flat per-pool rate skips, not a market survey.

vs-skimmer.html.text:
← Pool route pricing calculator

This calculator vs. Skimmer

Different jobs: one runs the route business day to day, the other decides what the accounts on it should be charged.

Skimmer is a well-known pool service business platform, described on getskimmer.com — optimized weekly routing and scheduling, a technician mobile app for logging chemical readings and service visits per body of water, invoicing and payment collection, and back-office reporting. It is the kind of software a pool service company runs its whole operation through, day after day, account after account.

That is a different job from the one this page does. This calculator has no account, no route map, no service log and no invoicing. It exists for the step that comes before any of that software is useful: turning your service minutes, drive minutes, labor rate, chemical cost and route overhead into a minimum monthly account price, and checking whether the price you currently charge actually clears your target margin once the drive is counted.

What each tool answers

Where to answer each question.
QuestionWhere to answer it
What is the minimum I should charge per account, given my labor, drive time, chemicals, and overhead? This calculator — it returns a specific price floor and shows the route hours and cost behind it.
Is my current price actually covering the route, or losing money once drive time is counted? This calculator — enter your current price and it checks it against the same floor.
How do I lay out an efficient weekly route across my accounts? Route software such as Skimmer — optimized routing and stop sequencing are jobs this page does not attempt.
Where do technicians log chemical readings and service visits per pool? Route software such as Skimmer — per-visit service and chemical logs live there, not here.
How do I invoice accounts and collect payment reliably every month? Your route and billing software. This calculator only tells you what number to put in it.
Is a given monthly price allowed by my local licensing, water-care, or contract rules? Neither. That is a question for your own advisers and local regulations, and no calculator settles it.

The same split applies whatever you run your route on. Skimmer, a spreadsheet, or a paper route sheet are all places a price can live; none of them is where the price comes from. If you already pay for route software, keep it — this page is not an alternative to it, and switching is not the point.

What this page deliberately does not tell you: what Skimmer or any other platform costs, which plan includes which feature, or how their routing and billing tools are configured. Those change, and a stale figure repeated here would mislead you. Check the platform's own site for that, and check this calculator for the price you are going to load into it.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Skimmer?

Both, for different jobs. Skimmer is pool service business software: routing and scheduling, service and chemical logs per body of water, invoicing and payments, and a technician mobile app, run through a paid account. This page is none of that. It has no account, no route map, no service log and no invoicing. It answers the one question that software asks you to already know rather than answers: what should the minimum monthly account price actually be, given your labor, drive time, chemicals, and overhead. Put those numbers in and it returns a specific price floor, the route hours behind it, and what your current price is leaving on the table if it falls short.

Where does the account price that goes into route software come from?

From you. Route and billing software stores whatever monthly price you set per account and then invoices it reliably every cycle, which is genuinely the hard part of running a route business day to day. What it cannot do is tell you whether that price actually covers your true route cost, including the drive time between stops that no customer is billed for directly. That is the gap this calculator fills, and it is why the two sit next to each other rather than competing.

Is this page affiliated with Skimmer?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Skimmer or any other pool service software named on this page. Those names appear only to describe what this calculator is and is not. Each is a trademark of its respective owner. Check any platform's own site for what its current plans and features actually include, because this page deliberately publishes none of their prices or feature details.

Open the pool route pricing calculator to work out your own minimum price, then load it into whichever route software you already run. Nothing you type is uploaded.
